translation.title: The Slanderer (al-Humazah)
notes: English translation added as 'text_en' (segments, footnotes), 'lemma_en' (lemma headings) and '*_en' metadata fields; all original Arabic fields are unchanged. Segment boundaries follow the printed pages, so some sentences are split across segments. Qur'anic quotations are rendered in translation; transliterated reading variants are given in parentheses.

x: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Commentary on the Surah "Woe to every slanderer" (Surat al-Humazah).
On the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted, whose names are sanctified:

Woe to every scorner and backbiter (humazah lumazah) (1) who amasses wealth and counts it over (2) He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal (3) No! He will surely be thrown into the Crusher (al-Hutamah) (4) And what will make you know what the Crusher is? (5) It is the fire of God, kindled (6) which rises over the hearts (7) Indeed, it will be closed upon them (8) in extended columns (9)
. He, mighty be His mention, means by His saying
: a valley that flows with the pus and discharge of the people of the Fire.
: He says, to every one who slanders people, who speaks ill of them and reviles them
: "You offer me affection, when you meet me, falsely … yet if I am absent, you are the slanderer, the backbiter (al-hamiz al-lumazah)."
By "lumazah" He means one who finds fault with people and attacks them.
The people of interpretation have spoken in line with what we have said on this.
Mention of those who said that: Musharraf
ibn Aban related to us, saying:

c: Waki' related to us,
m: , from a man he did not name, from Abu al-Jawza', who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: Who are these
people whom God began with woe? He said: They are those who walk about with tale-bearing, who separate loved ones, who seek out the greatest faults

c: Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from his father, from a man of the people of Basra, from Abu al-Jawza', who said:
m: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: Who are these people whom God has consigned to woe? Then he mentioned something like the report of Musharraf

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid:
m: . He said: The humazah is one who eats people's flesh, and the lumazah is the fault-finder
. Something contrary to this view has also been reported from Mujahid, namely what Abu Kurayb related to us, saying:

c: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid:
m: . He said: The humazah is the fault-finder, and the lumazah is one who eats people's flesh
ibn Aban al-Khattab related to us, saying:

c: Waki' related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid,
m: the same. And a view contrary to both of these has also been reported from him, namely what Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying:

c: Yahya related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid:
m: . He said: One of them is the one who eats people's flesh, and the other is the fault-finder. And this indicates that the one who transmitted this report was unsure about the interpretation of the two words, which is why what the narrators related from him differed in the way I have mentioned.

c: Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah:
m: : as for the humazah, he is one who eats people's flesh, and as for the lumazah, he is the one who attacks them.

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, who said:
m: The humazah is one who eats people's flesh, and the lumazah is the one who attacks them.

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan,
m: , from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas:
. He said: Woe to every fault-finder who slanders

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said:
m: The humazah is the one who slanders him to his face, and the lumazah
the one who does so behind his back

c: Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said:
m: He slanders him and reviles him with his tongue and his eye, eats people's flesh, and attacks them

c: Al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying:
m: related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: The humazah is with the hand, and the lumazah is with the tongue

x: Others said something different on this, as Yunus related to me, saying:

c: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:
m: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the saying of God:
: The humazah is the one who pokes people with his hand and strikes them with his tongue, and the lumazah is the one who taunts them with his tongue and finds fault with them
. There was also disagreement over who is meant by His saying:

x: Some said: a particular man among the polytheists is meant. Some of those who held this view said: He is Jamil ibn 'Amir al-Jumahi.
Others among them said: He is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.
Mention of those who said that a particular polytheist is meant:

c: Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas,
m: . He said: A polytheist who used to taunt people and slander them

c: Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Waraqa' related to us,
m: both together from Ibn Abi Najih, from a man of the people of al-Raqqah, who said: It was revealed concerning Jamil ibn 'Amir al-Jumahi.

c: Al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Waraqa' related to us,
m: . He said: It is not specific to anyone; it was revealed about Jamil ibn 'Amir. Waraqa' said: al-Raqqashi claimed it.

x: Some of the people of Arabic

said: This is of the kind where the Arabs mention a general noun, and it intends a single person, as is said in speech when a man says to someone: I will never visit you, (and the other says:) whoever does not visit me, I am not his visitor. The one who says this intends a reply to his companion who said to him: I will never visit you.
refers to everyone who has this attribute, with no other particular intent.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Waraqa' related to us,
m: both together from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, on the saying of God:
. He said: It is not specific to anyone

. The correct view on this is to say: God has made the statement general, covering every humazah lumazah; everyone who has the attribute with which this described person is described, his course is the same course, whoever

x: Who amasses wealth and counts it over

. He says: the one who amasses wealth and tallies its number, but does not spend it in the way of God and does not pay what is due to God from it; rather he amasses it, stores it away and guards it. The reciters differed in how they read this. Among the reciters of Medina, Abu Ja'far, and the general body of the reciters of Kufa except 'Asim, read it (jammaʿa) with doubling of the m
, while the general body of the reciters of Medina and the Hijaz other than Abu Ja'far, the general body of the reciters of Basra, and, from Kufa, 'Asim, read
; and all of them agree on doubling the d in

, in the sense of its interpretation that I have mentioned. It has been reported of some of the early authorities, with a chain of transmission that is not firm, that he read it (jamaʿa malan waʿadadahu) with the d undoubled
, meaning: he amassed wealth and amassed his clan and his numbers.
This is a reading I do not permit myself to recite by, because it goes against the reading of the major centers and departs from what the consensus of the authorities holds on this. As for His saying

: both the doubled and the undoubled forms are correct, because they are two well-known readings among the reciters of the major centers, close in meaning, so whichever of them the reciter reads, he is right.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in how they read this.

Among the reciters of Medina, Abu Ja'far, and the general body of the reciters of Kufa except 'Asim, read it (jammaʿa) with doubling of the m (4), while the general body of the reciters of Medina and the Hijaz other than Abu Ja'far, the general body of the reciters of Basra, and, from Kufa, 'Asim, read {jamaʿa} without doubling (1); and all of them agree on doubling the d in {waʿaddadahu}, in the sense of its interpretation that I have mentioned.

It has been reported of some of the early authorities, with a chain of transmission that is not firm, that he read it (jamaʿa malan waʿadadahu) with the d undoubled (2), meaning: he amassed wealth and amassed his clan and his numbers.
This is a reading I do not permit myself to recite by, because it goes against the reading of the major centers and departs from what the consensus of the authorities holds on this.

As for His saying {jamaʿa malan}: both the doubled and the undoubled forms are correct, because they are two well-known readings among the reciters of the major centers, close in meaning, so whichever of them the reciter reads, he is right.

x: He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal
. He says: he thinks that his wealth, which he has amassed and counted up and been miserly in spending, will make him immortal in this world and so remove death from him! The past tense

was used, though the meaning is "will make him immortal (yukhliduhu)", just as it is said of a man who does something that becomes a cause of his ruin: "By God, so-and-so has perished," and "By God, so-and-so has been destroyed," meaning that he will perish from what he did, though he has not yet perished or been destroyed; and like the man who commits one of the deadly sins: "By God, so-and-so has entered the Fire."

. He, mighty be His mention, says: It is not as he thought; his wealth will not make him immortal. Then He, glorified be His mention, informed that he is doomed and will be punished for his deeds and the sins he used to commit in the world, and so He, glorified be His mention, said:
He will surely be thrown into the Crusher (al-Hutamah)

. He says: he will surely be hurled on the Day of Resurrection into the Hutamah. The Hutamah is one of the names of the Fire, as it is also called Jahannam, Saqar and Laza. I think it was so named because it crushes (hatm) everything thrown into it, just as a man who is devoured is called "a Hutamah." It is reported of al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read this as (layunbadhanni fi al-Hutamah), meaning this humazah lumazah and his wealth, and so he put the verb in the dual for that reason

evidence.text: It is reported of al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read this as (layunbadhanni fi al-Hutamah), meaning this humazah lumazah and his wealth, and so he put the verb in the dual for that reason (1).

x: And what will make you know what the Crusher is?
. He says: And what has made you aware, Muhammad, of what the Hutamah is?

c: Then He informed him
m: what it is, and so, glorified be His mention, said: It is
the fire of God, kindled (6) which rises over the hearts

. He says: the one whose pain and blaze rise up over the hearts. Rising up (ittila') and reaching (bulugh) can have the same meaning; it has been reported from the Arabs, by hearsay: "When did you reach (talaʿta) our land?" and "I reached (talaʿtu) my land," meaning, "I arrived."

x: Indeed, it will be closed upon them
. He, mighty be His mention, says: Indeed the Hutamah whose attribute I have described is,
, meaning upon these slanderers and backbiters,
, meaning covered over and shut. The word may be pronounced with the hamza or without it, and we have all been taught both readings
The people of interpretation have spoken in line with what we have said on this.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Talq related to us, from Ibn Zuhayr, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas,
'Ubayd ibn Asbat related to me, saying: My father related to me, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from 'Atiyyah,

x: Indeed, it will be closed upon them

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ya'qub related to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said:
m: In the Fire there is a man, in one of its ravines, who cries out for the span of a thousand years: "O Hannan, O Mannan!" Then the Lord of Might says to Gabriel: "Bring My servant out of the Fire." So he comes to it and finds it covered over, and returns and says: "My Lord,
indeed, it is closed upon them
." He says: "Gabriel, open it and bring My servant out of the Fire." So he opens it, and the man comes out like a phantom, and he throws him
on the shore of Paradise until God makes hair, flesh and blood grow for him

c: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan,
m: Indeed, it will be closed upon them

c: Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Mudarris ibn 'Abd Allah, who said:
m: Indeed, it will be closed upon them

c: Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas:
m: Indeed, it is closed (muʾsadah) upon them

c: Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah:
m: Indeed, it is closed upon them

c: Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:
m: Ibn Zayd said, on His saying:
Indeed, it is closed upon them
: Covered over. And the Arabs say: "awsada al-bab" meaning, he shut the door.

x: . The reciters differed in how they read this. The general body of the reciters of Medina and Basra read
with fatha on the 'ayn and the mim
, while the general body of the reciters of Kufa read (fi ʿumudin) with damma on the 'ayn and the mim

. The position on this in our view is that they are two well-known readings, each of which learned reciters have read, and two sound dialects: the Arabs form the plural of 'amud (column) as both 'umud and 'amad, with damma on both letters or fatha on both. They do likewise in the plural of ihab (hide), forming ahub, with damma on the alif and ha', and ahab, with fatha on both; and likewise qadim
. So whichever of them the reciter reads, he is right.
The people of interpretation differed on the meaning of this.
Some of them said: [the meaning is]
: that it is closed upon them with extended columns, that is, locked and covered over them. Such is also the reading of 'Abd Allah, as has reached us

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Qatadah,
m: on the reading of 'Abd Allah: (innaha 'alayhim muʾsadatun bi-ʿamadin mumaddadah)

x: Others said: Rather the meaning is that they were put into columns, then those columns were extended over them with pillars.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas:
m: . He said: He put them into columns, which were then extended over them with pillars, with chains around their necks, so the doors were sealed with them

c: Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said:
m: : of iron, in which they are shackled, and those columns are of fire, burned by the fire so that they are fire themselves,

x: Others said: They are columns with which they are tormented.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah:
m: : We used to be told that they are columns with which they are tormented in the Fire
. Bishr said: Yazid said: in the reading of Qatadah:

c: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah:
m: . He said: a pillar with which they are tormented in the Fire. The most correct of these

views is the view of those who said that its meaning is that they are tormented with columns in the Fire. And God knows how He tormented them with them; no report has come to us that constitutes proof about the manner of their torment with them, nor has any evidence been set up for us with which we could grasp the nature of that, so no view on it other than what we have said is sound in our opinion. End of the commentary on Surat al-Humazah.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in how they read this.

The general body of the reciters of Medina and Basra read {fi ʿamadin} with fatha on the 'ayn and the mim (1), while the general body of the reciters of Kufa read (fi ʿumudin) with damma on the 'ayn and the mim (2).

The position on this in our view is that they are two well-known readings, each of which learned reciters have read, and two sound dialects: the Arabs form the plural of 'amud (column) as both 'umud and 'amad, with damma on both letters or fatha on both.
Such is also the reading of 'Abd Allah, as has reached us (5).
Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Qatadah, on the reading of 'Abd Allah: (innaha 'alayhim muʾsadatun bi-ʿamadin mumaddadah) (6).
Bishr said: Yazid said: in the reading of Qatadah: {ʿamad}.

notes.en: This is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar, Yaʿqub, and Hafs from ʿAsim. See al-Nashr (2/301).
notes.ar: هي قراءة ابن كثير ونافع وأبي عمرو وابن عامر وأبي جعفر ويعقوب وحفص عن عاصم. النشر 2/ 301.

notes.en: This is the reading of ʿAsim in the narration of Abu Bakr, Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Khalaf. See the preceding source.
notes.ar: هي قراءة عاصم في رواية أبي بكر عنه وحمزة والكسائى وخلف. المصدر السابق.

notes.en: Manuscript M reads “al-qadm,” while T2 and T3 read “al-ʿasm.” Al-qadim is white leather; its plurals include qudum and qudam. See Lisan al-ʿArab, root q-d-m.
notes.ar: في م: "القضم"، وفى ت 2، ت 3: "العصم". والقضيم: الجلد الأبيض، يجمع على قُضُم وقَضَم. اللسان (ق ض م).

notes.en: Manuscript M omits it.
notes.ar: سقط من: م.

notes.en: See al-Qurtubi’s Tafsir (20/185). Ibn Khalawayh attributed this reading in Mukhtasar Shawadh al-Qurʾan (p. 180) to al-Aʿmash.
notes.ar: ينظر تفسير القرطبي 20/ 185 ونسب هذه القراءة ابن خالويه في الشواذ ص 180 إلى الأعمش.

notes.en: Ibn Rajab mentioned it in al-Takhwif min al-Nar (p. 86), and Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (8/502), from Qatadah with this chain. ʿAbdullah’s reading is anomalous because it conflicts with the written form of the codex.
notes.ar: ذكره ابن رجب في التخويف من النار ص 86، وابن كثير في تفسيره 8/ 502 عن قتادة به. وقراءة عبد الله شاذة لمخالفتها رسم المصحف.

notes.en: Here ends the lacuna in the original Qarawiyyin manuscript mentioned on p. 469.
notes.ar: =إلى هنا ينتهى الخرم من مخطوط جامعة القرويين (الأصل) المشار إليه في ص 469.

notes.en: Ibn Rajab mentioned it in al-Takhwif min al-Nar (p. 87), and Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (8/502), from al-ʿAwfi with this chain. Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/393) to the author.
notes.ar: ذكره ابن رجب في التخويف من النار ص 87، وابن كثير في تفسيره 8/ 502 عن العوفى به، وعزاه السيوطي في الدر المنثور 6/ 393 إلى المصنف.

notes.en: Manuscripts S and T1 read “mamdudah.”
notes.ar: في ص، ت 1: "ممدودة".

notes.en: Ibn Rajab mentioned it in al-Takhwif min al-Nar (p. 88).
notes.ar: ذكره ابن رجب في التخويف من النار ص 88.

notes.en: ʿAbd al-Razzaq transmitted it in his Tafsir (2/395) from Maʿmar, from Qatadah. Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/393) to ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.
notes.ar: أخرجه عبد الرزاق في تفسيره 2/ 395 عن معمر عن قتادة، وعزاه السيوطي في الدر المنثور 6/ 393 إلى عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر.

notes.en: Manuscript M omits it.
notes.ar: سقط من: م.

notes.en: The original reads “biha.”
notes.ar: في الأصل: "بها".
